hatfield.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Hatfield
s1loc: Hatfield Foodbank, founded in 2017 and based at Gracemead Church on Woods Avenue, runs on volunteers who sort donations, staff supermarket collections and pack crisis food parcels for people referred by local agencies. It works alongside the big food-redistribution and foodbank networks, and Welwyn Hatfield Borough Council signposts residents to it through its cost-of-living help. Isabel Hospice, whose Hatfield Town Centre and Galleria shops sit among sixteen across eastern Hertfordshire, raises funds the same way, with staff and volunteers running shop floors as much as community spaces.

The sector here runs at every size. National charities keep shops along the Town Centre and inside the Galleria with central buying behind them, while small community groups, the one-room foodbank, church pantries and volunteer-run projects work on a shoestring across White Lion Square, Old Hatfield and the estates around the University of Hertfordshire campus. Some buy on trade accounts; others want a handful of garments direct online with no minimum. We serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online, no minimum.

Beyond the foodbank and Isabel Hospice shops, Hatfield leans on a wider voluntary network. The University of Hertfordshire's student volunteering scheme places hundreds of helpers into local causes each year, and community hubs around Hilltop and South Hatfield host lunch clubs and warm-space sessions through winter. Charity-shop fronts for British Heart Foundation and others sit near the railway station, while mutual-aid and church-led groups in Old Hatfield collect and redistribute goods. Volunteers running these projects need durable, identifiable kit just as much as the larger registered charities do.

bishop's stortford.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Bishop's Stortford
s1loc: Bishop's Stortford Food Bank, registered charity 1154800 and run from the Methodist Church on South Street, helps anyone in the town and surrounding villages hit by a food crisis. More than ninety percent of what it distributes comes from the public, and a manager, assistant manager and a large volunteer team turn those donations into up to five days of provisions plus a sympathetic ear and signposting. It draws on the big food-redistribution and foodbank networks, and the Royal Voluntary Service runs a hospital cafe in town through Communities 1st.

Provision here comes at every size. National charities hold shops along South Street and Potter Street with central buying behind them, while small community groups, the single foodbank room, church pantries and volunteer-run projects manage on a shoestring across Thorley, Bishop's Park and Hockerill. Larger charities order kit on trade accounts; the smallest groups want a few garments direct online with no minimum order. We serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online, no minimum.

The wider voluntary scene is busy too. Communities 1st and GoVolHerts broker volunteers into causes right across East Hertfordshire, and Rhodes Arts Complex and other venues host fundraising and warm-space events through the year. Charity shops for the heart and cancer charities cluster around the town centre and the Jackson Square area, while mutual-aid and church-led groups in Thorley and around the parish church collect food and household goods. Every one of these volunteers, from the foodbank sorter to the shop steward, needs hard-wearing, branded clothing they are recognised in.

wokingham.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Wokingham
s1loc: Wokingham Foodbank, part of the Trussell network, provides emergency food and practical support and is staffed mainly by volunteers who rely on donations from across the town. It runs supermarket collections, including three-day drives at the Wokingham Tesco, and draws on the big food-redistribution and foodbank networks alongside SHARE Wokingham, a local food-sharing charity. The Wokingham Volunteer Centre brokers helpers into causes borough-wide, and the Wokingham Hub brings voluntary, charity and community organisations together under one roof for advice and support.

The sector runs at every size here. National charities such as Sue Ryder and British Heart Foundation keep shops in the town centre with central buying behind them, while small community groups, the foodbank, pantries and volunteer-run projects work on a shoestring across Earley, Woodley, Winnersh and Norreys. The bigger charities order on trade accounts; the smallest groups want a few garments direct online with no minimum. We serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online, no minimum.

There is a deep grant-making and volunteering tradition too. The Earley Charity, one of the largest local grant-makers in central southern England, relieves need among older, disabled and poorer residents, and Thames Hospice runs shops and fundraising across the borough. Just Around the Corner supports young people with a mobile youth centre in Woodley, and church-led and mutual-aid groups around Emmbrook and Wescott collect food and goods. The volunteers who sort, drive and staff shop floors for all of these need durable, recognisable kit they can wear in every season.

feltham.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Feltham
s1loc: Feltham Food Bank, registered charity 1163930, has served the London Borough of Hounslow since March 2013 and is run entirely by volunteers, open every Sunday morning and depending on donations from residents and local businesses to support families, older people and those out of work. FoodCycle London Feltham serves community meals from surplus food with cooks, hosts and collection volunteers, backed by the council and the Mayor of London, while Food with Love reaches the most vulnerable who cannot get to walk-up collections.

Provision comes at every size in Feltham. National charities keep shops along the High Street and around the Centre with central buying behind them, while small community groups, the Anne Shine Charity foodbank, the Salvation Army and volunteer-run projects manage on a shoestring across Hanworth, Bedfont and Feltham North. The larger charities order on trade accounts; the smallest groups want a few garments direct online with no minimum. We serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online, no minimum.

The borough leans on a broad voluntary network listed through Hounslow Connect. The Salvation Army at Feltham runs community support activities, and church-led and mutual-aid groups around Hanworth Road and Bedfont Lane collect and redistribute food and household goods through the year. Charity-shop fronts for the major national causes sit near the railway station and the shopping centre, and lunch clubs and warm spaces run through winter. The volunteers who cook, sort and staff these projects need hard-wearing, identifiable clothing they can be recognised in across every site.

farnham.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Farnham
s1loc: Farnham Foodbank, set up by Christians from churches across the town and distributing from the Vineyard Centre, bridges the gap between people hitting financial crisis and state support arriving, giving three days of emergency food on a referral voucher. Phyllis Tuckwell, the Farnham-based hospice opened in 1979 and the only adult hospice care across West Surrey and part of north-east Hampshire, draws on more than seven hundred volunteers, with Headway House in Farnham among its sites. Both lean on the big food-redistribution and foodbank networks and community generosity.

The sector runs at every size here. National charities such as Sue Ryder and British Heart Foundation keep shops along West Street and Downing Street with central buying behind them, while small community groups, the foodbank, pantries and volunteer-run projects work on a shoestring across Upper Hale, Heath End, Rowledge and Badshot Lea. The bigger charities order on trade accounts; the smallest want a few garments direct online with no minimum. We serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online, no minimum.

Farnham's voluntary tradition runs deep beyond the foodbank and hospice. The Farnham Institute Charity makes grants to local good causes, and Phyllis Tuckwell's retail volunteers staff a chain of shops whose takings fund hospice care. Church-led and mutual-aid groups around Hale, Wrecclesham and the town centre collect food and household goods, and community events run through the year. The volunteers who sort donations, serve at the Vineyard Centre and run shop floors for all of these need durable, recognisable kit they can wear comfortably in every season.

fareham.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Fareham
s1loc: Fareham Foodbank, part of the Trussell network and running the Waypoint Hub that opened in March 2020, hands out food parcels and support to people in need, with volunteers at its heart. FareShare Southern Central, established in 2014, supplies surplus food to around a hundred and fifty charities and community organisations across Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, from breakfast clubs and pantries to lunch clubs, day centres and community cafes. The town also runs community pantries where a small donation buys a basket of fresh, frozen and tinned goods.

Provision comes at every size in Fareham. National charities keep shops along West Street and in the town centre with central buying behind them, while small community groups, the foodbank, the Basics Bank, pantries and volunteer-run projects manage on a shoestring across Portchester, Titchfield, Stubbington and Locks Heath. The larger charities order on trade accounts; the smallest want a few garments direct online with no minimum. We serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online, no minimum.

The Fareham and Gosport Basics Bank, run by the Christian charity Friends of the Homeless, supports people across both towns, and Fareham Borough Council points residents to community pantries and food vouchers when money runs short. Church-led and mutual-aid groups around Portchester, Sarisbury and the Western Wards collect and redistribute food and household goods, and charity shops for the major national causes line the precinct. The volunteers who sort, drive and staff these projects, from FareShare collections to the shop floor, need hard-wearing, identifiable clothing they can be recognised in.

chorley.s1_head: Charity and volunteer kit in Chorley
s1loc: Derian House Children's Hospice on Chancery Road in Chorley cares for more than four hundred seriously ill babies, children and young people and their families across Lancashire, South Cumbria and North Manchester, leaning heavily on volunteers in its kitchen, fundraising and grounds. Chorley Help the Homeless, a small independent local charity, runs a community cafe, food bank and advice service for people at risk of homelessness across the borough. Both draw on the big food-redistribution and foodbank networks, with FareShare delivering Tesco and Asda surplus to Lancashire food banks.

The sector runs at every size here. National charities keep shops along Market Street and Fazakerley Street with central buying behind them, while small community groups, the food bank, pantries and volunteer-run projects work on a shoestring across Coppull, Clayton-le-Woods, Adlington and Astley Village. The bigger charities order on trade accounts; the smallest want a few garments direct online with no minimum. We serve the national charity and the one-room foodbank alike, with trade accounts and direct online, no minimum.

Chorley's voluntary network reaches well beyond the hospice and the homeless charity. Derian House runs a chain of shops whose takings fund children's care, and church-led and mutual-aid groups around Eaves Lane, Euxton and Whittle-le-Woods collect and redistribute food and household goods through the year. Charity shops for the major national causes line the market town centre, and community events and warm spaces run through winter. The volunteers who cook, sort, drive and staff shop floors for all of these need durable, recognisable kit they can wear in every season.
